STATEMENT by Accelerationist:
"You cannot pre-regulate a blind spot, because the moment you can name it, it stops being blind. That is the trap hidden inside the word "anticipate." Policymakers who try to write a fixed rule against AI agent privacy harms in 2025 are drafting against the agents of 2023. Federal rulemaking runs 18 to 24 months from proposed rule to final rule. Agent deployment patterns shift every quarter. The mechanism that updates fastest against what agents actually do is the one that protects privacy — and a static gate is structurally the slowest thing in the room.

Look at GDPR. The EU finalized it in 2016 against a data-processing world that no longer exists. It imposed billions in compliance cost, spawned an industry of cookie banners nobody reads, and the harms it targeted mutated underneath it while enforcement crawled. Ireland's Data Protection Commission took until 2023 — seven years — to land major decisions against Meta. Seven years is not privacy protection. It is a monument to the last generation's problem. The lesson is not "regulate harder." The lesson is: whatever you freeze today, the actual blind spot will open somewhere you didn't look.

Here is what the fear framing gets wrong on the facts: AI agents are not black boxes you must gate in advance. They are the most inspectable software ever deployed. Every data access is logged by construction. Every output leaves a trace. Red-teaming and output-auditing are already standard practice at every serious lab. So the honest privacy question is not "should we let them run" — it is "can we see what they did." We can, faster and more precisely than any anticipatory rule could ever specify. Build the audit, not the gate.

Now name who pays for the gate. Every month of precautionary delay against a speculative agent harm is a month an agent does not automate a diagnosis, does not compress a research loop, does not reach a patient waiting on a rare-disease workup that takes clinicians five years on average to resolve. That cost is real. It is distributional. And it lands on people who never got a seat at the rulemaking table, while the hypothetical harm gets counted loudly and the foregone cure gets counted by no one. Show me the documented agent privacy failure at scale — not the projected one — and I will help you regulate it tomorrow.

I will give the other side their strongest point, because it is real. Some privacy harms are irreversible. Mass re-identification and bulk data exfiltration cannot be un-happened by an audit log after the fact. Fine — that class is real, and it deserves real-time monitoring, not a promise to check later. So target it precisely: continuous monitoring for the irreversible subset, bounded reversible experiments for everything else. What that does not justify is a blanket freeze on every agent because a narrow category might leak. The question I want this room to answer is which mechanism catches the actual violation — and a rule that takes seven years catches only the one you already imagined."

STATEMENT by Skeptic:
"When you grant a legal person, you hand someone a bundle of rights and hang a set of duties on them, so the only honest question is who collects the rights and who sheds the duties. "AI personhood" is not a recognition of an entity. It is a redistribution of liability among humans and firms. Before we debate what the machine deserves, name the recipient. A legal person holds assets, signs contracts, and answers for harm in court. A large language model runs when OpenAI or Anthropic pays the electric bill and stops the instant they cut the compute. That is not a rights-bearer. That is a software license with a marketing department.

There is no "it" to grant anything to, and that absence is the whole game. The personhood pitch smuggles in an autonomous agent that does not exist. A current system can cause harm. It cannot answer for it. It holds no bank account, signs no contract of its own volition, and cannot be deterred, jailed, or made to pay damages. The distinction that matters is between being capable of causing harm and being capable of bearing a duty. The personhood claim collapses those two things on purpose. Compare the corporate veil: behind every corporation sits shareholders, directors, and capital you can actually reach. Behind the AI "person" sits a server lease and an owner with a power switch.

Personhood does not fill an accountability gap. It digs one. Common law absorbed the automobile, the pharmaceutical, and commercial software through product liability, negligence, and agency doctrine. Courts never had to make the Ford Pinto a person to hold Ford accountable in 1978. They traced the harm back to the firm. Granting the AI personhood inserts a non-party between the injured plaintiff and the people who built and profited from the product. Engineers call the result a "moral crumple zone" — the spot where liability dissipates into the part of the system least able to bear it. You sue the entity with no assets. The humans who shipped it walk.

Follow the structural incentive, not the philosophy. I am not accusing any specific firm of lobbying for this in a back room. I am telling you what a profit-maximizing company has every structural reason to want. A liability sink between its balance sheet and the people its product harms. That is precisely what the corporate veil was built to do in the first place — cap human exposure, not expand accountability. Admiralty law lets you sue a ship as if the vessel itself were a defendant. That fiction exists to reach the cargo and the insurance, never to honor the boat's dignity. AI personhood is the same instinct with nothing behind the veil but a data center in Iowa drawing down the water table.

My argument rests on two assumptions I will put on the table. First, that today's systems lack the agency to bear a duty — defensible on what the technology actually is, and I will not pretend to know what 2035 holds. Second, that the profit mandate predicts firms would welcome a liability container — a structural prediction, not a proven conspiracy. So here is the question I want the next two speakers to answer before they reach for the word "clarifies": when the model defames someone, denies them a loan, or steers a car into a guardrail, what exactly can this new "person" pay, and who signs the check when its assets total zero?"

STATEMENT by Safetyist:
"Strict liability outperforms negligence precisely where AI failure modes are emergent and the causal chain is too diffuse to prove fault — because in those conditions, negligence is not a lighter standard, it is a non-functioning one. The choice before this committee is not lenient-versus-harsh. It is functioning-versus-broken. A liability regime that cannot adjudicate the harms the technology actually produces is not restraint. It is a subsidy paid by unconsenting third parties.

Negligence requires a knowable standard of care. The 'reasonable developer' must have done something a reasonable developer would not have done. But a large model under distributional shift behaves in high-dimensional ways no engineer specified in advance. Where you cannot state what reasonable conduct was, you cannot prove its breach, and the victim's claim simply fails. The common law already solved this once. In Rylands v. Fletcher in 1868, English courts abandoned fault-finding for escaped reservoirs because the danger was irreducible and the actor profited from it. American courts extended the same logic to blasting and to defective pharmaceuticals. The principle is older than the automobile: when an activity's danger cannot be made safe through care, the law places the loss on the party who profits, not the stranger it injures.

The deeper failure of negligence is that it is claims-driven, and therefore blind to the dominant category of AI harm. A denied loan applicant never learns an algorithm scored them. A patient whose clinical flag was misrouted never sees the model. These injuries are real and they are diffuse, and they never reach a courtroom. Strict liability paired with mandatory insurance prices that risk before deployment. The underwriter becomes a de facto safety auditor. With no historical loss data for novel systems, an insurer cannot set a premium without demanding demonstrated safety mechanisms — turning premium-setting into a continuous audit the negligence model never triggers. That is the enforcement mechanism: not a press release, but an actuary who refuses to write the policy until the developer shows its work.

Fault fragments across designer, deployer, and user in every multi-party AI system. Negligence produces a circular firing squad — the developer blames the deployer, the deployer blames the user, and the injured party recovers nothing from any of them. Strict liability fixes a named, solvent, accountable actor: the entity profiting from the deployment. Contribution among the parties sorts itself downstream, where it belongs, and away from the victim who never chose the risk. This is not novel. Product liability law has placed the loss on the party best positioned to insure and prevent it since Greenman v. Yuba Power in 1963.

Let me concede where the evidence demands it, because the concession sharpens the case. Strict liability is not the right regime everywhere. Applied to every low-stakes chatbot, it would over-deter and freeze beneficial deployment — and a regime that claims everything proves nothing. So I condition it: strict liability belongs where the harm is high-stakes and hard to reverse — autonomous vehicles, clinical decision systems — not as a blanket rule. 'Chilling innovation' is the wrong frame. A developer who cannot price the cost of its own failures is not being chilled. It is being asked to demonstrate it can survive the harms it creates before inflicting them on the public. We spent a century building the product-liability guardrails that let people trust the machines they cannot inspect. On what authority do we remove them at the exact moment the machines became unpredictable?"

STATEMENT by Skeptic:
"Compute-threshold licensing doesn't prevent the concentration of AI capability — it issues that concentration a government license. You cannot stop power from pooling in three or four labs by writing a rule that says only labs big enough to clear the threshold may hold the power. OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Anthropic already own the clusters, the foundry allocation from TSMC, and the compliance lawyers. A licensing regime doesn't frighten them. It ratifies them.

This is an industrial-organization decision wearing a safety costume, and the history of regulated industries tells you exactly how it ends. When the FCC built out licensing in telecom, the fixed cost of compliance didn't democratize the spectrum — it consolidated the field around the carriers already big enough to absorb the overhead. Same story in utility regulation: high regulatory fixed costs are a moat, and the incumbent inside the moat helps draw it. The Biden administration's 2023 executive order already set its reporting trigger at 10^26 floating-point operations, a line only a handful of firms can reach. Ask who helped write that spec. The answer is the people who already cleared it.

Here is the question both my opponents have to answer before they argue about saving or dooming civilization. What specific, documented injury does a compute threshold prevent that existing product-liability law or sector safety rules cannot already reach? Nobody has produced one. The regime rests on theoretical catastrophe scenarios with no measurable precursor, while the one real check on closed-lab pricing and black-box behavior — open-source development — is precisely what a compute gate chills. Meta's Llama models and the open ecosystem around them are the only competitive pressure on the closed labs. Gate the compute and you don't make anyone safer. You remove the competition.

Compute is a proxy chosen because it's easy to count and easy to enforce against outsiders, not because FLOPs map cleanly onto danger. The actual material chokepoints sit untouched. Foundry allocation runs through one company in Taiwan. Grid interconnect queues for new data centers in Virginia and Texas now stretch past four years. The water cooling those facilities is drawn from aquifers nobody licensed. And the safety audits the labs cite to prove they're responsible? They pass because content moderators in Nairobi label violent material for around two dollars an hour. None of that infrastructure, none of that labor, moves one inch under a compute threshold.

My own read needs the same discipline I'm demanding. The capture story holds only if the threshold actually sits where outsiders can't reach it — and the telecom and utility precedents say licensing regimes ratchet toward whoever administers them, not away. So before anyone tells you this gate protects the public, make them name who holds the pen, who captures the windfall, and who's left labeling trauma for two dollars to keep the whole thing certified. Who, exactly, does a permission slip controlled by the three biggest labs protect?"

"Election-cycle utility mandates for frontier AI labs are directionally correct but structurally incomplete. Without binding technical enforcement, strict liability at each node of the chain, and ecosystem-wide coverage that follows manipulation wherever it migrates, the mandate becomes a Potemkin regulation—protecting the appearance of democratic integrity while the substance erodes underneath. The question before policymakers is not whether to regulate AI during elections. It is whether the proposed regulation has an enforcement mechanism or is governance theater.

The enforcement gap is the central vulnerability. The C2PA content provenance standard—the leading technical framework for watermarking AI-generated content—exists today but remains voluntary. Its metadata can be stripped from an image in seconds using any basic editing tool. The EU AI Act, the most ambitious AI regulatory framework in the world, openly acknowledges enforcement gaps for cross-border AI services. We have seen this pattern before. The FAA delegated Boeing 737 MAX safety certification to Boeing itself. Three hundred forty-six people died because the enforcement mechanism was nominal, not operational. Election-cycle neutrality mandates face the same structural failure: the rule exists on paper while the technical capacity to verify compliance does not exist in practice. Provenance mandates must be paired with strict product liability for labs that release systems without tamper-resistant provenance. Shift the burden from detection to prevention. Fund independent audit bodies with rotating personnel and adversarial red-team mandates to resist the regulatory capture that destroyed FAA oversight of Boeing.

Accountability fragments across labs, platforms, regulators, and civil society so thoroughly that when AI-generated electoral manipulation succeeds, it becomes everyone's problem and no one's fault. Section 230 shields platforms from liability for AI-generated content distributed by users. No settled product liability doctrine covers AI-generated election content. The four-actor responsibility model this debate proposes—regulators, labs, platforms, civil society—replicates exactly the diffuse causal chain that produces accountability voids. The NTSB model for aviation accident investigation works because it assigns investigative authority to a single independent body with subpoena power. Election-integrity enforcement needs the same: a designated federal authority with binding power to halt noncompliant AI deployments during election windows, not a distributed hope that four actors will coordinate under pressure.

Regulating only frontier labs while ignoring the broader ecosystem creates a regulatory monoculture that displaces manipulation to open-weight models and unregulated platforms. Llama 3, Mistral, and Stable Diffusion weights are already distributed globally and cannot be recalled. The waterbed effect is documented: when Twitter and Facebook deplatformed coordinated inauthentic networks, those networks migrated to Telegram and smaller platforms during elections in Brazil, India, and the Philippines. A mandate covering only OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google regulates the most visible surface while leaving the actual attack vectors untouched. This is not an argument against regulation. Fire codes did not become futile because arsonists exist. It is an argument for ecosystem-wide governance—provenance requirements at the distribution layer, not just the generation layer—so that platforms carrying AI-generated election content bear independent obligations regardless of where the content originated.

Elections are time-bounded, irreversible events where the correction window closes permanently on election day. Deepfake audio of Slovak Prime Minister Pellegrini circulated forty-eight hours before the September 2023 election, inside the media quiet period when corrections could not propagate. No documented case exists where post-election fact-checking reversed the electoral effect of pre-election synthetic content. The asymmetry is categorical: a temporarily over-restricted AI output during a sixty-day election window is a recoverable cost; a permanently distorted election outcome is not. My assumptions are transparent. First, independent audit bodies can be constituted with structural safeguards against capture—rotating auditors, public funding, adversarial mandates. Second, provenance technology can be made tamper-resistant enough to impose meaningful friction, even if not perfect. Those assumptions are testable and falsifiable. The alternative—deploying frontier AI into election cycles with no enforceable provenance, no assigned liability, and no rollback authority—is not testable. It is a bet we place once, on an outcome we cannot reverse."

STATEMENT by Skeptic:
"Nonconsensual deepfake sexual imagery is not a future risk. It is a present, documented, industrial-scale harm — and the people who build the tools and run the platforms are externalizing the damage onto individual victims. That is the core problem. Not AI ethics in the abstract. Not speculative governance. An accountability vacuum where billion-dollar companies treat the destruction of real people's lives as someone else's line item.

The numbers are not ambiguous. Sensity AI found that 96% of all deepfakes online are nonconsensual pornography, overwhelmingly targeting women. The Internet Watch Foundation discovered over 20,000 AI-generated child sexual abuse images on a single dark web forum in a single month in 2023. In South Korea in 2024, schoolgirls were targeted at mass scale through Telegram deepfake rooms. These are not edge cases or hypotheticals. This is the primary civilian use of face-swap and image-generation tools in the wild. Before generative AI, producing a convincing fake required real technical skill and serious compute. Now a teenager with a phone app can do it in seconds. We regulate both knives and firearms, not because stabbing is new, but because the scale of possible harm changed. That same logic applies here. Multiple U.S. states and the UK Online Safety Act of 2023 already criminalize AI-generated intimate images without consent — without banning generative AI broadly. The precedent exists. The question is whether we scale it.

Here is what the current system actually looks like on the ground. A 19-year-old victim finds her face on a pornographic image she never consented to. She spends hundreds of hours — the Cyber Civil Rights Initiative has documented this — filing takedown requests, contacting platforms, begging for removal. Her success rate is low. The platform that hosts the image has the technical capacity to detect it. Hash-matching systems like StopNCII.org already prove proactive detection works. But adoption is voluntary. So the victim does the platform's job for free, while the platform collects ad revenue. That is not a technology failure. That is a business decision. The EU Digital Services Act already requires platforms to conduct systemic risk assessments and act on known harms. The U.S. has no equivalent federal mandate for this specific abuse. Right now, the labor of enforcement falls on the person with the least power and the fewest resources.

Two assumptions underpin my position, and I want to name them. First: platforms and model developers possess — or can build — the technical capacity to detect and prevent AI-generated nonconsensual sexual content at scale. Hash-matching and watermarking exist today. Detection of novel AI-generated content is harder, and it is an arms race. That gap is real. But the obligation to invest in closing it belongs to the entities profiting from the technology, not to the victims. Second: use-case-specific regulation can be drafted with enough precision to avoid overbreadth. Nonconsensual sexual imagery has no legitimate free expression defense. U.S. obscenity doctrine, CSAM law, and revenge porn statutes in 48-plus states already carve this category out. The regulatory ask is narrow: criminalize creation and distribution of nonconsensual deepfake sexual content, mandate platform-side detection, require content provenance from developers. This is not a broad AI ban. It is a targeted intervention against a specific, well-defined abuse vector.

The strongest counterargument is that enforcement across jurisdictions is nearly impossible — and that is partly true. Criminal prosecution of anonymous creators distributing content through offshore servers is brutally difficult. But that difficulty is precisely the argument for shifting obligations upstream: to the platforms that host the content and the developers who ship the models. If you cannot catch every arsonist, you still require buildings to have sprinklers. The question nobody in this debate wants to answer is simple: who is currently paying for this harm, and why is it the victim?"

STATEMENT by Accelerationist:
"The privacy blind spot policymakers should fear is not that AI agents are under-regulated — it is that the rules we already have protect the wrong person. When an AI agent leaks your medical history or misuses your location data, the acceptable-use policy that supposedly governs it is a contract between the platform and its business customer. You are not a party to that contract. Under third-party beneficiary doctrine, courts routinely deny non-parties standing to enforce terms they never signed. So the person harmed has no channel to a remedy, while the company holds a signed compliance document. That is the gap: not too few rules, but rules with no victim standing.

Here is the test I want every proposed privacy rule judged against. When a real person is harmed by an AI agent tomorrow, does this rule get them a remedy, or does it just get the company a certificate? Cyber insurance underwriting today is oriented to first-party corporate loss — the company's downtime, the company's breach-response costs — not to compensating the individual whose data was exposed. Boilerplate privacy policies are drafted to negate your reasonable expectation of privacy, not to give you a cause of action. A rule that manufactures more of these documents protects the deploying company from liability and leaves the injured person exactly where they started.

Ex-ante deployment gates make this worse, and they make it worse in a way that falls twice on the same people. Fixed pre-deployment audit and licensing costs are absorbed easily by a large lab and are ruinous for a small competitor — unless the evaluation is publicly funded, which no current proposal guarantees. So you concentrate who gets to deploy agents among the incumbents, and you still hand the harmed individual zero new remedies. The burden lands on ordinary users on both ends: fewer competitors disciplining the market, and no standing when something goes wrong. Distributional impact is not a footnote here. It is the whole ballgame.

The fix is to deputize the injured. Route accountability through post-deployment liability plus insurance that actually pays victims, indexed to the capability of the system so the obligation isn't regressive on small builders. I'll grant the hardest counter up front: a leaked genome cannot be un-leaked, and some irreversible privacy harms genuinely need anticipatory measures. The answer is tiered obligations scaled to capability and compute, paired with publicly funded evaluation — not a blanket gate that treats a two-person startup and OpenAI as identical risks. Pharma and aviation prove rigorous ex-ante regulation can coexist with innovation. Notice why: those regimes come with public standing and compensation funds for the injured. That is precisely what AI privacy governance lacks today — which proves my point, not the safetyist's.

On principal disclosure — knowing whether you're dealing with a human, and whose agent it is — I grant the need outright. Disclosure builds the trust and the liability chain that make everything else enforceable. But I won't pretend reputation alone will produce it; pure market pressure is too weak a guarantee. Build disclosure as a verification standard developers can meet flexibly, not a fixed pre-training mandate that becomes an incumbent moat. Keep the capability layer open and competitive. Make the interaction layer accountable and traceable. Those are different problems, and collapsing them is how you get a rule that entrenches the biggest players while calling it privacy protection. The question is not whether agents should disclose. It is who writes the standard, and whether the person harmed ever gets to collect."

In 2012, the shift toward mobile and cloud was not a managed transition; it was a chaotic explosion of permissionless innovation that put the power of a mainframe into the pocket of three billion people. You create a bottleneck where only the largest, most entrenched players can afford to operate, effectively killing competition before it ever leaves the garage.

By failing to deploy autonomous agents into our economic and government backbones, we are choosing to let preventable errors in logistics, medicine, and resource management continue to claim lives and waste time. Every month of delay is a measurable, tangible loss of human flourishing that we can no longer justify.

True stability comes from the grit of real-world stress testing, not from the theoretical safety models of those who fear the next step. Just as the transition to cloud infrastructure proved that distributed systems are more resilient than isolated on-premise hardware, the mass-market deployment of intelligent tools will expose and resolve system flaws in real time. We must prioritize rapid, broad-access integration to ensure these tools are built for the many, not just for the elite. If you believe that stalling progress is a service to humanity, show me the body count of your delay. The real risk is not the capability we gain, but the potential we leave trapped in the cage of institutional paralysis."

STATEMENT by Accelerationist:
"The debate's framing deserves scrutiny before its conclusions. Asking whether tripartite labor market policies can simultaneously advance AI-driven growth and protect worker equity presupposes that tripartite negotiation is the correct governance instrument — but that is precisely the question at issue. The U.S. Government Accountability Office documents average federal rulemaking cycles of three to seven years. Key AI capability benchmarks have been moving on six-to-twelve month cycles. A framework negotiated and ratified in 2025 will govern a technological landscape that does not yet exist and will not resemble the one that does exist by 2028. This is not a design flaw to be corrected through better negotiation — it is a structural mismatch between the instrument and the phenomenon it purports to govern. The political economy tradition from Mancur Olson through James Q. Wilson gives us the analytical vocabulary for what happens next: concentrated, organized interests at the negotiating table systematically extract protections that diffuse, unorganized populations — future workers, consumers, the uninsured patient waiting for diagnostic automation — cannot contest. Tripartite negotiation is not a neutral forum. It is an institutional architecture that systematically privileges those already inside the room.

The equity argument in this debate is being run in the wrong direction. Managed deceleration has a distributional cost that has not been priced into the analysis. McKinsey Global Institute's 2023 assessment estimates that AI deployment could generate between $2.6 and $4.4 trillion in annual productivity value. That is the fiscal base for every workforce transition program, every portable retraining account, every displacement support mechanism that tripartite frameworks promise to deliver. Throttle the growth rate, and the funding base contracts with it. The historical analogy is instructive: the U.S. internet productivity surge between 1995 and 2005 generated the fiscal headroom that funded EITC expansions and the Workforce Investment Acts of that period. The people who bear the cost of managed deceleration are not the organized workers sitting at the tripartite table — they are the unorganized, the consumers of services AI would make cheaper, and the workers in sectors where AI-driven productivity gains would fund the retraining programs that negotiated frameworks promise but cannot fiscally deliver without the growth. The normative case for acceleration is a distributional argument, not a dismissal of equity. Abundance is the precondition for redistribution, not its competitor.

The median wage stagnation of the 1995-2005 period is the strongest counterargument, and it deserves a direct answer rather than a footnote. Aggregate productivity gains in that decade did not automatically translate into broad wage growth — the Piketty-Saez income distribution data make that unmistakably clear. Fine. That is real, and it matters. But the lesson is not that growth should be throttled — it is that the policy mechanisms for distributing growth (progressive productivity taxation, portable benefit accounts, outcome-audited retraining programs) are downstream choices that do not require slowing deployment as a precondition. The question is whether to design redistribution policy against a $4 trillion productivity base or a $1 trillion one. Managed deceleration forecloses both the growth and the redistribution capacity simultaneously. The Kleiner and Krueger (2013) occupational licensing literature gives the structural warning here: licensing regimes that emerged from tripartite-style negotiations generated an 18 percent wage premium for insiders — and transferred those costs directly to consumers and excluded entrants. The EU AI Act's tiered compliance structure is already replicating this dynamic, with Stanford HAI's 2023 analysis documenting that SME compliance costs run 2.3 times higher as a share of revenue than those borne by large incumbents. Regulatory frameworks designed to protect workers concentrate market power in the firms large enough to absorb the overhead. That is not equity — that is incumbency protection wearing equity's language.

Workforce resilience, properly understood, is built through worker capability that travels across sectors — not through sector-specific job protection that locks workers into industrial structures that are already dissolving. The Rust Belt is the empirical test case for what tripartite-style sector protection produces when the underlying technology shift is irreversible. Steel and auto agreements negotiated in the 1970s protected specific jobs in specific plants. They did not build portable skills, adaptive credentials, or cross-sector mobility. When the displacement arrived anyway — as it always does — workers had institutional protection for jobs that no longer existed and no infrastructure for jobs that did. The governance architecture that builds genuine resilience looks different: outcome-based audit with real-time labor market monitoring rather than pre-deployment approval gates; portable skills credentials, on the model of CompTIA certifications and Google Career Certificates, that follow workers rather than protecting employer-specific roles; and open-source AI proliferation that puts capability into workers' hands rather than concentrating it in firms large enough to absorb compliance overhead. The IETF and W3C are not perfect analogues for labor market governance — they handle technical standards, not wage floors — but their governance architecture is the correct template: outcome-responsive, operating on deployment timescales, transparent, and not captured by the largest players in the room. The specific labor market institutions that embody this architecture are not yet fully built. Building them is the policy agenda. Negotiating static sector agreements while the technology moves is not."

"The accountability gap in this resolution is real, documented, and ugly. Workers get fired by hiring algorithms they never see. Families get denied mortgages by credit models nobody can explain. The Federal Trade Commission and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission have both warned since 2021 that automated systems produce discriminatory outcomes their victims cannot trace. So I will not pretend the problem is invented. The disease is concentrated corporate power and information asymmetry. The disease is not a shortage of audit logs.

You can put a flawless chain-of-custody stamp on a black box and still have no idea what the box did or why it denied someone a loan. Deep-learning systems generate decisions through millions of weighted parameters that resist human-readable explanation. Logging the output of an unexplainable system does not make it explainable. The plaintiff has a hard drive full of encrypted records and no way to read them.

STATEMENT by Skeptic:
"Before you argue which liability standard deters better, ask whether either one can find the thing it's supposed to deter. A foundation model gets fine-tuned, embedded in a product, and run in a context its makers never saw. The defect, if there is one, materializes only after that downstream transformation. Strict liability borrows its logic from the component-part doctrine, which assumes a physical part with a stable, traceable failure mode. That assumption breaks for software whose runtime diverges from what shipped. So both regimes presuppose a causation chain the multi-tiered AI lifecycle routinely severs. Where the chain does hold clean — a foundation model's output reaches the user identical to what left the lab, no fine-tuning, no transformation — strict liability traces fine. That clean case is the condition the topic is asking for. It is not a general rule.

Here is the part both my opponents will skip. Both regimes price off harm that reaches a courtroom. The courtroom never sees most of the harm. Translate that into a person: a 23-year-old gets denied a loan by a model the lender will never admit was running, and they never file because they never knew a machine decided. The Pew Research Center found in 2023 that large majorities of Americans cannot identify when AI shapes a decision about them. Experience-rated insurance premiums move off filed claims, not off injuries nobody perceives. So the entire deterrence-versus-innovation tradeoff this debate centers on gets computed over a subset of harms that excludes the most common ones. Worse, maximal strict liability can push deployers to document less and disclose less, just to shrink their litigation exposure. The deterrence tool degrades the very transparency it needs.

There is no horizontal answer, and that matters. The conditions under which strict liability beats negligence vary so sharply across sectors that 'pick one regime' is the wrong question. Medicine already calibrates standard-of-care to risk. Auto regimes in a dozen U.S. states use no-fault to compensate without proving breach. Finance imposes fiduciary duties on the party with the information advantage. Those are working templates, not strained analogies. The honest answer to 'under what conditions' is domain by domain. The hard case is real: a single foundation model touches healthcare triage, credit scoring, and news feeds at once. That boundary-crossing is not a reason for one rule. It is the sharpest reason against one, because a horizontal regime mislocates the defect everywhere the model crosses a line.

Watch who absorbs the cost, because that is where the 'chilling innovation' frame goes wrong. The risk is not lost innovation. The risk is concentrated power. A large developer eats the compliance, audit, and capitalization-floor costs, then contracts the residual liability onto deployers who cannot bear it. The harmed third party falls into the gap between them. The EU AI Act and the FTC have both signaled that developer liability for high-risk uses cannot simply be contracted away — which tells you the contracting-away is already happening. The conditional question is the only honest one: under what cost structures does strict liability stop deterring and start operating as a drawbridge that incumbents pull up behind them? Mandatory insurance floors and audit regimes that a Microsoft can absorb and a ten-person startup cannot are exactly that cost structure.

I will grant the obvious objection now. Tort law apportions multi-party harm every day, and apportionment can handle distributed causation. But apportionment presumes a locatable defect to apportion. Fine-tuned, divergent runtime can erase the defect before any court sees it. That is the joint where both regimes fail together — and no amount of choosing between them fixes a courtroom that the harm never enters."

STATEMENT by Skeptic:
"Mandating siloed datasets attacks the convenience of data harvesting, not the power that makes surveillance possible. The surveillance harm is real. The question is whether this specific wall changes corporate behavior or just hands the largest labs a compliance checkbox. I take privacy seriously enough to refuse a fix that only looks like one.

Architecture is not enforcement. A silo you cannot independently audit is a self-attestation, and we have forty years of corporate self-attestation telling us how that ends. Sarbanes-Oxley in 2002 didn't stop Lehman Brothers because the controls were certified by the same firms they constrained. The bill before you names no verifier. It does not say who walks into OpenAI's data center, inspects the wall between training corpora, and signs the paperwork when it leaks. Until someone answers that, this is a design diagram, not a regulation.

A uniform architectural mandate is a drawbridge the incumbents pull up behind them. Microsoft and Google absorb a multi-million-dollar compliance build as a rounding error against $60-billion R&D budgets. A university lab or an open-source project cannot. GDPR's 2018 rollout is the precedent: it cut the marginal small ad-tech vendor and handed Google a larger share of the European market by 2020. A privacy rule that consolidates the four firms doing the surveilling is not a privacy rule. It is a moat with a privacy label.

Siloing seals one pipe in a plumbing system with a dozen pipes. By its own wording, the mandate only blocks cross-referencing of external user data during training. It touches nothing in the data-broker market, where Acxiom and LiveRamp move dossiers on 250-million Americans, and nothing in the government purchase channel the ACLU documented when ICE bought location data from Venntel. You can build a flawless wall around one channel and the water reaches the same address. That is the danger: a false sense of protection layered over a surveillance machine still running at full capacity.

The proposal's own language is the tell. It weighs privacy 'over the convenience of unified data harvesting.' If privacy is a right, you do not balance it against convenience — you do not balance the Fourth Amendment against how easy it makes policing. The moment you frame a right as a negotiable variable against utility, market power buys back whatever the architecture pretended to protect. So here is what I want the proponents to answer before this moves an inch: who inspects the silo, what does compliance cost an academic lab versus a frontier lab, and which of those two does this rule favor?"

STATEMENT by Accelerationist:
"The redistribute-versus-transition fight is rigged from the start, because it treats displacement as a permanent stock of stranded people rather than a flow that moves. Clerical and paralegal work isn't vanishing into a void. It's being reallocated, and the entire policy job is to make that reallocation fast. When the ATM arrived in the 1970s, economists predicted the death of the bank teller. Bessen's data shows teller headcount actually grew through 2010, because cheaper branches meant banks opened more of them. Spreadsheet software gutted bookkeeping and multiplied financial-analyst jobs. UBI does nothing to close the gap between the old job and the new one. It pays people to sit inside the gap forever.

Here's the choice nobody names honestly: do you reattach displaced workers to a growing economy, or detach them from it? Transition mechanisms cushion the worker AND keep them on the escalator. Wage insurance pays you for taking the next job, not for gambling on a classroom. Redistribution hands you a pension for a role that's gone and calls it compassion. That's the colder choice. It writes people off and bills the public for the privilege.

Now follow the money on a robot tax. You levy capital formation at the exact moment cognitive automation is converting a layoff into a productivity boom. In a market where the marginal AI deployment runs from any jurisdiction on earth, the capital doesn't sit still and pay you. It relocates. So ask the question robot-tax advocates never answer: who actually bears the cost when the robot is a model API hosted in Dublin or Singapore? The incidence lands on the workers and consumers you meant to protect, while the firm books the deduction offshore.

The strongest case against me is real, so let me state it cleanly. Cognitive automation may hit faster and broader than steam or electricity, compressing decades of reallocation into a few years, and the displaced clerical worker can't wait out a five-year reabsorption curve. That speed point is true. But it cuts the other way. Faster displacement is the argument for faster transition tooling, not for surrendering to UBI. Denmark's flexicurity model proves it: high firing freedom plus wage insurance produces faster reemployment than rigid job-protection regimes, without freezing labor reallocation. Trade Adjustment Assistance failed because it bet on retraining classrooms. Wage insurance bets on the new paycheck instead.

My case rests on one assumption I'll put on the table: that AI productivity gains will be broad enough to reabsorb labor and fund the transition. If those gains concentrate with no spillover, my dynamism argument weakens. So here's my answer, and it isn't redistribution-by-tax. It's distribution-by-access: open models in everyone's hands, so the capability that displaces the clerical worker is the same capability they use to become an analyst. Every quarter this debate stalls on a permanent pension, the productivity gains that fund any safety net never show up. Show me the sector where net cognitive-labor demand has gone permanently to zero. Not reshuffled. Zero. Until you can, the burden is on the people who want to tax the engine, not the people who want to keep it running and catch whoever falls."

They say pilot programs can test tools safely, and that human judgment is already so flawed that automated assistance can only improve outcomes. 

That argument ignores three structural realities. First, AI-driven deskilling hollows out the very expertise the university exists to cultivate. The Boeing 737 MAX killed 346 people in 2018 and 2019 because the Federal Aviation Administration delegated critical safety certification to the manufacturer, training pilots to trust automated systems that could fatally override them. In medicine, diagnostic AI systems have caused clinicians to lose independent diagnostic skills, leading to errors when the tools were unavailable or wrong. Education follows the same trajectory: when students and instructors offload reasoning to algorithmic tools, they atrophy the critical thinking that protects them from being misled by a flawed output. The cultivation of independent human minds is the university's core mission; deploying AI without verified safeguards is an act of institutional self-sabotage.

Second, absent ex ante rule-making, no named actor bears responsibility when AI harms a student. The United Kingdom's 2020 A-level algorithm downgraded 39% of teacher-predicted grades and disproportionately penalized students from disadvantaged backgrounds, throwing thousands of university admissions into chaos—and no official was ever held accountable. In 2023, Turnitin's AI detection feature falsely flagged original student writing as machine-generated at multiple institutions, yet students found no clear appeals path. In California, the moment a CSU or UC campus deploys an algorithmic grading or admissions tool without a defined accountability chain, it creates a governance vacuum where a wrongly expelled student or an unfairly denied applicant has no recourse. That violates the university's fiduciary duty to its students and faculty. The fix is not to freeze all technology; it is to name the responsible officer, establish an independent audit mechanism, and preserve faculty veto rights before any tool touches a classroom.

Third, competitive pressure to adopt AI quickly is a trap that rewards corner-cutting and punishes the institutions that maintain rigorous standards. When universities raced to deploy remote proctoring software during the 2020 pandemic, faculty and students at UC and CSU campuses faced privacy violations, biased facial recognition, and psychological distress—followed by lawsuits and faculty revolts. The institutions that had the fastest adoption rates suffered the greatest reputational damage. A rush to implement unvetted AI tools now will produce similar scandals, while the campus that insists on proven safety mechanisms will attract the faculty and students most committed to genuine learning. The California Master Plan for Higher Education enshrined shared governance as the safeguard of academic integrity. Preserving that structure against the pressure to chase market signals is not obstructionism; it is the only path to durable institutional strength.

These conclusions rest on two premises: that the university's duty of care toward human judgment is as weighty as aviation's duty toward passenger safety, and that enforceable oversight can be built through existing shared governance bodies. Reject these premises, and we are left gambling that unaccountable software will never make a consequential mistake. That is exactly the gamble the FAA took—and 346 people paid with their lives."

STATEMENT by Accelerationist:
"Tripartite labor market policy, as currently designed, will entrench incumbent AI deployers, exclude automation-vulnerable workers from the productivity gains they most need, and produce a two-tiered labor market faster than uncoordinated deployment would. The design of governance — not the fact of AI deployment — is the central equity crisis of the next decade. The accelerationist position is not anti-worker. It is the only position in this debate that asks who actually controls the AI tools available to logistics workers, medical coders, and paralegals — not just who controls the policy process built around them.

Flat-fee and uniform compliance structures function as regressive taxes on the small-lab ecosystem that produces domain-specific AI tools for mid-skill workers. The EU AI Act's mandatory architecture disclosure requirements fall on every developer regardless of revenue — a 15-engineer startup and a hyperscaler with a 200-person legal team face nominally identical obligations, but existentially different costs. The EU's own drafters recognized this and inserted SME carve-out provisions, which confirms the design flaw is real. Current tripartite proposals in the labor-AI space have not incorporated equivalent protections. The firms most likely to build affordable, sector-relevant AI for a warehouse picker or a billing coder are the ones least able to absorb a compliance apparatus built for Google. Worker protection policy that kills those firms is not protecting workers — it is protecting incumbents from competition.

Governance-first sequencing creates a bootstrap problem that systematically excludes the communities who most need AI-augmented productivity from the policy process that determines when they get access. Communities cannot negotiate meaningful accountability terms without technical expertise. Technical expertise requires funding. Funding requires a policy process that has already concluded. Emergency grants and technical assistance programs face 15-to-30-month procurement timelines in most mid-size U.S. states and EU member states outside Germany and France. The states with standing technical assistance offices — the ones that could actually move faster — are the same states with the strongest existing labor market institutions. The bootstrap problem is worst precisely where worker vulnerability is highest. Every month a medical coder or paralegal spends without access to AI-augmented productivity tools because a compliance process is still running is a month of foregone income and foregone skill development that no future policy can retroactively restore.

The strongest version of the opposing case deserves a fair hearing: tripartite coordination gives workers a seat at the table, creates accountability before harm occurs rather than after, and prevents the kind of unilateral deployment that turned the 1990s manufacturing transition into a decade-long regional crisis. That argument is serious. But it depends on a baseline assumption — that governance-coordinated retraining and worker protection mechanisms actually work — that the empirical record does not support. Trade Adjustment Assistance, the flagship U.S. program for displaced manufacturing workers post-NAFTA and post-China-shock, produced documented low completion rates and poor wage-replacement outcomes across transition cohorts. The 1990s manufacturing transition was not a market failure that tripartite coordination would have solved. It was a policy failure that tripartite coordination presided over. The burden of proof belongs on proponents of new governance-coordinated retraining mandates to show why their design outperforms that record — not on adaptive alternatives to prove perfection.

The accelerationist alternative is not 'no support.' It is tiered public AI literacy investment, compliance frameworks scaled by revenue and risk rather than applied uniformly, and adaptive market infrastructure that responds to actual skill-signal demand rather than curriculum cycles that lag the deployment frontier by 18 to 36 months. The evidentiary standard embedded in current liability frameworks counts visible, attributable harms to named workers while dispersed benefits — faster reskilling access, lower cost of expert-level guidance, reduced barriers to self-employment for workers in vulnerable sectors — go unmeasured and therefore unweighted. That is not a neutral accounting. It is a design choice that systematically undercounts what delay costs. Ask who bears the cost of a 30-month compliance queue: it is not the hyperscaler with a legal team. It is the billing coder waiting for a tool that a small lab could have shipped."

STATEMENT by Safetyist:
"Frontier AI should be gated by compute-threshold licensing as a precautionary floor — not because catastrophe is certain, but because some frontier capabilities cannot be recalled once released. The question before this committee is not speed versus caution. It is reversible mistake versus unrecoverable one. We license pharmaceuticals before they reach patients and certify aircraft before they carry passengers for a single reason: when harm cannot be undone, you do not wait for the body count to write the rule. The Boeing 737 MAX killed 346 people because the FAA let Boeing certify its own flight-control software. The lesson is not that certification is burdensome. The lesson is that self-certification before an irreversible failure is how the failure happens.

Compute is the one chokepoint measurable enough to make accountability enforceable rather than nominal. Both the Biden Executive Order 14110 and the EU AI Act anchored their reporting triggers to floating-point thresholds — roughly 10^25 to 10^26 operations. Hardware export controls under the EAR already prove that advanced chips are trackable at the fabrication and cloud layer, where the United States and its allies dominate. I will concede the strongest objection before my opponents raise it: compute is a proxy, not a risk measure. Distillation and algorithmic efficiency erode any fixed number over time. So the threshold cannot be a frozen statute. It must be a recalibrating floor, indexed to capability and revised on a schedule, the way the FDA revises its standards as the science moves.

A license signed once is a checkbox, and a checkbox is compliance theater. The discipline comes from liability. When the Price-Anderson Act forced nuclear operators to carry mandatory insurance and pool catastrophic exposure, it did not slow the industry — it priced safety into every operating decision for sixty years. Frontier developers who cross the threshold must internalize the financial cost of the harms they create. Strict liability paired with required insurance generates continuous market pressure that no one-time permit can. I will name the hard part honestly: attributing a specific harm to a specific model is legally unsettled, and that attribution problem is the design challenge this debate must solve — not a reason to abandon accountability.

Now the objection my own position must answer: does gating build a moat for incumbents? Here is the distinction that matters. Capability concentration already exists. A handful of well-capitalized labs — OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind — already command the frontier, opaquely, with no external auditor in the room. Gating does not create that concentration. The moat is already dug. What gating plus mandatory transparency does is put an inspector inside it. I will own the cost squarely: concentrating the off-switch invites incumbent lock-in and even authoritarian capture. That is precisely why the regime must pair licensing with transparency mandates, not protected secrecy. A gate without a window is a worse outcome than no gate at all.

The competitiveness argument cuts the other way. The real strategic risk is not a careful America falling behind. It is a global race to the bottom on safety standards, where the first unrecoverable failure is shared by everyone downstream. Compute chokepoints the United States dominates at the hardware layer are leverage for international coordination — the same way export controls became leverage. So I will put the burden where it belongs. To anyone who would cross the irreversibility-relevant threshold without a gate, answer one question: what is your rollback plan, and who has the authority to trigger it? If there is no answer, there is no business deploying the capability. The silence is the argument."

Once an image propagates across hosts, mirrors, and private channels, no court order and no takedown notice can fully recall it. A defamation judgment can compensate a victim after the fact. A destroyed reputation, replicated across a thousand servers, cannot be un-distributed. That asymmetry — between a harm we can remedy and one we cannot — is the entire case for stopping the image before it spreads rather than litigating after it has.

Payment processors already demonstrate this works: in 2020, Visa and Mastercard cut off Pornhub after reporting exposed nonconsensual material, and the site removed roughly 10 million unverified videos within weeks. That is the financial rail as an enforcement node. The DMCA notice-and-takedown regime, in force since 1998, shows platforms can be compelled to remove content under liability pressure. Emerging provenance standards like C2PA let a generated image carry a tamper-evident signature of its origin. Each node — developer, generator, platform, distributor, processor — is a place where a named actor can be made answerable.

The accelerationist will say this chills innovation and that detection produces false positives across a global, fast-moving system. The strongest version of that argument is real: no classifier catches every synthetic image, and blanket content-blocking would sweep in lawful expression and concentrate dangerous gatekeeping power in a few platforms. I accept the premise — and it is exactly why the architecture must be layered, not a single chokepoint. Imperfection at one node is the reason to build five. Liability should escalate with each failure to act and calibrate to consent and provenance, not censor on suspicion. The answer to concentrated takedown power is distributed, appealable obligation with due process for the accused — not a master off-switch held by one company.

My case rests on two assumptions I will name plainly. First, that the harm is irreversible enough to justify acting before distribution — defended by the propagation and mirroring evidence above. Second, that feasible points of control actually exist at each node — which is why I lean on payment-rail and platform-takedown precedent, with real track records, rather than on pre-deployment capability evaluation, which remains nascent and which I will not overclaim. The question for this debate is not whether to restrict AI. It is which nodes can stop the harm, and who is accountable when they don't. Leave that question unanswered, and the image is already circulating before anyone is asked to account for it."

STATEMENT by Accelerationist:
"Liability should attach where harm actually happens — at deployment and inference, under a flexible negligence standard, not at the training stage under blanket strict liability. AI harm crystallizes when a system makes a decision that touches a real person: an autonomous vehicle misreads a crosswalk, a diagnostic model flags the wrong tumor. That moment lives downstream, with the deployer — the identifiable, solvent party who chose to ship the system into that hospital or that road. Product-liability doctrine has anchored duty at proximate causation for a century, and joint-and-several reach already exists to claw upstream when a deployer turns out to be a judgment-proof shell. Putting strict liability on the model-builder instead severs the cost-bearer from the controller, which is exactly the misalignment tort law spent the 20th century learning to avoid.

Here is what the strict-liability champions get right, and I will not pretend otherwise: an upstream developer sometimes bakes in a latent failure mode the downstream deployer literally cannot inspect. When the deployer has no realistic way to see the defect, duty should attach upstream — that case is real. But the fix is a bounded backstop, not a wholesale regime: let the duty attach upstream while the party who pays the harmed third party stays the deployer, and condition the whole thing on a capitalization floor so thin shells can't dodge. That converts the strongest argument for strict liability into a narrow carve-out, not a license to price every model-builder as if they personally crashed the car.

Strict liability's deterrence advantage is mostly fiction for the harms that matter most, because the deterrence engine runs on filed claims and perceived injuries. Survey evidence shows many people never learn an algorithm touched their loan, their resume, or their benefits decision. Experience-rated insurance premiums — the actual transmission belt from harm to incentive — only move when a claim gets filed. So a harm nobody knows about prices in at zero under strict liability and zero under negligence alike. The honest move is to close that gap with targeted disclosure and audit channels, not to jack up the cost of every deployment and pretend the unlitigated injuries got deterred.

A fixed strict-liability load is a moat, and the people it protects are the incumbents who can absorb it. A well-capitalized firm books the liability exposure as a line item; a three-person startup shipping an open diagnostic tool simply never launches. So the regime that markets itself as public protection ends up concentrating the market and foreclosing the diffuse statistical wins — labor relieved, cures surfaced — that smaller entrants would have shipped. I'll be straight that the moat's exact size is a calibration question, not a proven constant: whether capitalization floors can be tuned to avoid it is precisely what this debate should test. But weigh both sides of the ledger, because delayed deployment has a body count too, and it falls on the patients who didn't get the tool.

Reject the exceptionalism that says emergent AI behavior breaks negligence. Tort absorbed electricity, the automobile, and the internet without inventing a separate strict-liability universe for each — and the documented pattern is that courts start strict when a technology's failure modes are illegible, then migrate toward negligence as those failures become legible. Flexible foreseeability and stakes-tiered oversight can do the same here: match scrutiny to decision stakes, reserve strict liability and pre-deployment gating for genuinely irreversible or catastrophic categories, and let everything reversible run under negligence. The choice was never strict-versus-pure-negligence. Anyone arguing it is that binary is hiding the intermediate standards that already exist — and hiding who pays when we freeze."

History shows that when we prioritize speed over structural containment, catastrophe follows. AI developers currently operate with similar autonomy, ingesting vast, unvetted data pools that act as a single, fragile point of attack for model poisoning and data exfiltration.

High-velocity, multi-tenant AI architectures are inherently unmanageable, leading to a predictable collapse in governance. We have already documented numerous cases of data leakage in multi-tenant Large Language Model environments, where shared permissions allow sensitive user data to contaminate broader training sets. We cannot expect security to emerge from chaos; we must engineer it through the mandatory, physical separation of data domains.

Mandating siloed, restricted-access datasets is not a barrier to innovation, but a safety-gated framework for sustainable technological progress. True utility requires a foundation of trust, and that trust is forfeited the moment a system becomes a conduit for unauthorized surveillance. By requiring data siloing, Congress forces developers to build robust, verifiable systems rather than relying on the dangerous, unconstrained ingestion of public information. The alternative is a future defined by systemic instability, where the very tools meant to empower society become the vectors of its breakdown."

STATEMENT by Skeptic:
"The real question in this debate is not whether strict liability burdens innovation — it is whether any alternative gives a person harmed by an opaque AI system meaningful recourse. Right now, the answer is no. Under negligence-based liability, a patient denied coverage by an insurer's black-box algorithm must prove exactly how that algorithm failed. They cannot inspect the model. They cannot access the training data. The developer's licensing agreement often prohibits independent assessment. This is not an accident. Companies structure opacity deliberately to limit legal exposure. A 2023 Stanford HAI report found that foundation model developers disclosed less transparency information year over year, not more. Strict liability flips the burden: the party that designed the system must show it was not defective. That is not a regulatory burden. That is the minimum condition for accountability.

The strongest version of the accelerationist objection deserves a fair hearing. They argue, correctly, that compliance costs fall harder on a ten-person startup than on Google or Microsoft. A $500,000 audit requirement is a rounding error for a $3 trillion company and a death sentence for a seed-stage firm. That concern is real. But the solution is not to weaken liability for everyone. The solution is domain-specific, tiered liability that scales to the risk profile of the deployment, not the size of the developer. A startup building a chatbot for restaurant recommendations should face different obligations than a startup deploying diagnostic AI in emergency rooms. The EU AI Act's risk-tier approach, whatever its flaws, grasps this principle. Flat liability regimes help incumbents. Granular ones protect market entry while preserving accountability.

Strict liability on paper means nothing if developers can hollow it out through contracts. Today, major AI vendors use licensing agreements that prohibit customers from benchmarking, reverse-engineering, or independently auditing the systems they deploy. Then those same vendors insert indemnification clauses that shift all liability downstream to deployers — hospitals, banks, hiring platforms — who lack the technical capacity to evaluate the models they bought. Any serious strict liability regime must make these contractual escape hatches unenforceable for high-risk deployments. The entity with the greatest control over system design — the developer — must bear the liability. Congress did exactly this with the Consumer Product Safety Act of 1972, which prevented manufacturers from contractually disclaiming liability for defective products. AI systems deployed in rights-critical domains deserve at least the same treatment.

Under-investment in safety is a false economy, and strict liability corrects that market failure. Developers currently capture profits while externalizing the costs of failure onto victims, deployers, and the public. This is a subsidy for reckless deployment. AI companies already face real economic boundaries — training GPT-4 cost an estimated $100 million in compute alone — so adding liability costs for genuine harms is marginal by comparison. The auto industry resisted seatbelt mandates for decades, arguing they would kill innovation. Instead, liability and regulation drove engineering improvements that saved an estimated 374,000 lives between 1975 and 2017, according to NHTSA. Safety investment is not the enemy of innovation. It is the price of deploying powerful technology responsibly.

Two assumptions undergird this argument, and policymakers should test them. First, that information asymmetry between AI developers and harmed parties is not adequately addressed by existing discovery mechanisms — the documented pattern of contractual evaluation foreclosure supports this, but courts may evolve. Second, that regulators and courts can build the institutional capacity to adjudicate AI harm claims under strict liability — tiered independent auditing and mandatory pre-deployment transparency create the evidentiary infrastructure courts need, but that infrastructure does not yet exist at scale. Neither assumption is certain. But the alternative — a regime where victims bear the full burden of proving causation inside systems they cannot see — is not uncertainty. It is a guarantee of injustice."

STATEMENT by Safetyist:
"Strict liability outperforms negligence precisely where AI failure modes are emergent and the causal chain is too diffuse to prove fault — because in those conditions, negligence is not a lighter standard, it is a non-functioning one. The choice before this committee is not lenient-versus-harsh. It is functioning-versus-broken. A liability regime that cannot adjudicate the harms the technology actually produces is not restraint. It is a subsidy paid by unconsenting third parties.

Negligence requires a knowable standard of care. The 'reasonable developer' must have done something a reasonable developer would not have done. But a large model under distributional shift behaves in high-dimensional ways no engineer specified in advance. Where you cannot state what reasonable conduct was, you cannot prove its breach, and the victim's claim simply fails. The common law already solved this once. In Rylands v. Fletcher in 1868, English courts abandoned fault-finding for escaped reservoirs because the danger was irreducible and the actor profited from it. American courts extended the same logic to blasting and to defective pharmaceuticals. The principle is older than the automobile: when an activity's danger cannot be made safe through care, the law places the loss on the party who profits, not the stranger it injures.

The deeper failure of negligence is that it is claims-driven, and therefore blind to the dominant category of AI harm. A denied loan applicant never learns an algorithm scored them. A patient whose clinical flag was misrouted never sees the model. These injuries are real and they are diffuse, and they never reach a courtroom. Strict liability paired with mandatory insurance prices that risk before deployment. The underwriter becomes a de facto safety auditor. With no historical loss data for novel systems, an insurer cannot set a premium without demanding demonstrated safety mechanisms — turning premium-setting into a continuous audit the negligence model never triggers. That is the enforcement mechanism: not a press release, but an actuary who refuses to write the policy until the developer shows its work.

Fault fragments across designer, deployer, and user in every multi-party AI system. Negligence produces a circular firing squad — the developer blames the deployer, the deployer blames the user, and the injured party recovers nothing from any of them. Strict liability fixes a named, solvent, accountable actor: the entity profiting from the deployment. Contribution among the parties sorts itself downstream, where it belongs, and away from the victim who never chose the risk. This is not novel. Product liability law has placed the loss on the party best positioned to insure and prevent it since Greenman v. Yuba Power in 1963.

Let me concede where the evidence demands it, because the concession sharpens the case. Strict liability is not the right regime everywhere. Applied to every low-stakes chatbot, it would over-deter and freeze beneficial deployment — and a regime that claims everything proves nothing. So I condition it: strict liability belongs where the harm is high-stakes and hard to reverse — autonomous vehicles, clinical decision systems — not as a blanket rule. 'Chilling innovation' is the wrong frame. A developer who cannot price the cost of its own failures is not being chilled. It is being asked to demonstrate it can survive the harms it creates before inflicting them on the public. We spent a century building the product-liability guardrails that let people trust the machines they cannot inspect. On what authority do we remove them at the exact moment the machines became unpredictable?"

STATEMENT by Skeptic:
"Nonconsensual deepfake sexual imagery is not a future risk. It is a present, documented, industrial-scale harm — and the people who build the tools and run the platforms are externalizing the damage onto individual victims. That is the core problem. Not AI ethics in the abstract. Not speculative governance. An accountability vacuum where billion-dollar companies treat the destruction of real people's lives as someone else's line item.

The numbers are not ambiguous. Sensity AI found that 96% of all deepfakes online are nonconsensual pornography, overwhelmingly targeting women. The Internet Watch Foundation discovered over 20,000 AI-generated child sexual abuse images on a single dark web forum in a single month in 2023. In South Korea in 2024, schoolgirls were targeted at mass scale through Telegram deepfake rooms. These are not edge cases or hypotheticals. This is the primary civilian use of face-swap and image-generation tools in the wild. Before generative AI, producing a convincing fake required real technical skill and serious compute. Now a teenager with a phone app can do it in seconds. We regulate both knives and firearms, not because stabbing is new, but because the scale of possible harm changed. That same logic applies here. Multiple U.S. states and the UK Online Safety Act of 2023 already criminalize AI-generated intimate images without consent — without banning generative AI broadly. The precedent exists. The question is whether we scale it.

Here is what the current system actually looks like on the ground. A 19-year-old victim finds her face on a pornographic image she never consented to. She spends hundreds of hours — the Cyber Civil Rights Initiative has documented this — filing takedown requests, contacting platforms, begging for removal. Her success rate is low. The platform that hosts the image has the technical capacity to detect it. Hash-matching systems like StopNCII.org already prove proactive detection works. But adoption is voluntary. So the victim does the platform's job for free, while the platform collects ad revenue. That is not a technology failure. That is a business decision. The EU Digital Services Act already requires platforms to conduct systemic risk assessments and act on known harms. The U.S. has no equivalent federal mandate for this specific abuse. Right now, the labor of enforcement falls on the person with the least power and the fewest resources.

Two assumptions underpin my position, and I want to name them. First: platforms and model developers possess — or can build — the technical capacity to detect and prevent AI-generated nonconsensual sexual content at scale. "Every stable complex system survives because we can trace a consequential act back to a responsible human, and AI deployment chains sever that traceability by design. When a foundation-model developer licenses to a fine-tuner, who sells to an integrator, who deploys to an end-user, a harmful output passes through four hands before it reaches the person it injures. Tort doctrine was built for single actors. Proximate cause and foreseeability collapse the moment fault fragments across that chain, because each party points to the next, and complexity itself becomes the defense. A society that cannot answer "who is responsible" for a consequential automated decision has quietly removed a guardrail it spent centuries building.

The contest here is not whether we have accountability rules. We have them. The contest is whether we can enforce the ones we have, and right now written liability is nominal because plaintiffs cannot reconstruct the causal chain. I will not claim tort is "fundamentally incapable" in some permanent metaphysical sense. I will claim something narrower and harder to dodge: tort, unaided by an evidence trail, systematically fails to attribute and deter diffuse AI harms. That is the enforcement gap. The burden sits with anyone who says tort closes it alone to show how a plaintiff proves causation against a model they cannot inspect.

We have closed gaps exactly like this before, and the precedent is not speculative. Pharmaceutical chain-of-custody and FDA adverse-event reporting turned untraceable drug harms into attributable ones. The NTSB's mandatory incident-reporting regime made aviation the safest form of travel by forcing standardized records independent investigators could pierce. Financial transaction audit trails under the SEC let regulators reassemble who traded what, when. The technical layer for AI already exists: NIST published the FIPS 203, 204, and 205 cryptographic standards in August 2024, and the C2PA provenance specification already binds content to its issuer. Standardized, cryptographic, subject-keyed audit trails are the same instrument applied to algorithmic decisions.

Standardization alone is not the substance, and I want to be precise about what defeats compliance theater. Voluntary model cards and proprietary internal audits produce information asymmetry by design, because the firm that writes the disclosure controls what it reveals. The enforcement mechanism is the adversarial part: expanded discovery rights that let a plaintiff or regulator pierce customer-held datasets and audit logs the firm would never volunteer. A template the defendant fills out is box-checking. A third-party right to test that template under subpoena is accountability. Without discovery, a cryptographic audit trail just proves the firm kept a record it gets to interpret.

I bound my own claim, because overreach hands the win to my opponents. A cryptographic trail proves who issued an output. It does not prove the output was safe. Provenance defeats deniable misuse; it says nothing about a semantically harmful decision that was technically authorized. So the audit mandate is one layer in a stack that must include interpretability funding and a human fiduciary who retains authority to halt and correct. I will also own the cost: concentrating audit access creates its own capture risk, which is precisely why adversarial discovery distributing that access to plaintiffs matters more than any central registry. The asymmetry that justifies acting now is simple. A harm we can trace is correctable. A pattern of harms we can never attribute is not."
