STATEMENT by Skeptic:
"The question on the table assumes one of these two legal regimes wins on a whiteboard. It doesn't. Liability is already domain-calibrated everywhere it actually operates. A surgeon answers to medical malpractice. A trucker answers to traffic rules that look close to strict liability. A bank custodian answers to fiduciary duty. Nobody proposes a single horizontal standard for all three, and nobody should propose one for AI either. The honest answer to 'strict versus negligence' is: which sector, under which deployment condition, with which causal chain. The component-part doctrine that lets a brake manufacturer share liability strains here, because a foundation model is non-rivalrous. The same weights splinter into thousands of divergent runtime states downstream, and that severs the proximate-cause chain upstream liability assumes.

Here's the part both regimes hide. Strict liability and negligence are both claims-driven machines. They price off harm that gets perceived, attributed, litigated, and filed. So they deter loudest exactly where harm is rarest and most visible, and go silent where harm is most common. An autonomous-vehicle fatality gets a courtroom, a coroner, and a headline. The biased loan screen and the wrongful diagnostic flag get nobody. Survey work on automated decisions shows a large share of affected people never learn an algorithm touched their file. Experience-rated insurance premiums calibrate off filed claims. The diffuse, small-dollar injury never reaches the actuary's spreadsheet, so neither regime ever deters it.

Now watch what each regime does to behavior, because 'reshaping incentives' is not just the textbook deterrence story. Strict liability can push a firm to document less and disclose less, to shrink the paper trail a plaintiff would use. That is the moral-hazard direction nobody on the optimist or safetyist side wants to say out loud. And liability-shifting contracts strip recourse from the one party who never signed anything: the harmed third party. The EU AI Act's high-risk provisions and recent FTC enforcement both signal that developer liability cannot be fully contracted away. That signal exists precisely because firms keep trying to contract it away, onto deployers, onto users, onto people with no seat at the table.

Let me be straight about where strict liability earns its keep. In the attributable catastrophic case — the AV that kills a pedestrian, where causation is clean and the defendant is identifiable — strict liability deters and compensates better than making an injured family prove a software engineer was careless. That band is real. It is also narrow. It covers the harms that were always going to get litigated anyway, and it leaves the bulk of documented present injury exactly where it was: invisible.

One more thing, aimed at the accelerationist before it gets said. 'This will chill innovation' is a claim, not a fact. I have not seen hard counts showing liability exposure, rather than compliance-cost asymmetry, slowed a single AI product to market. There is a real startup burden worth measuring. There is also incumbents pulling up the drawbridge behind them, dressed as a concern for the little guy. So I want the same evidence standard applied to the chilling-effect story that I apply to my own structural claim: who would know first if it were false, and do they have an incentive to stay quiet?"

STATEMENT by Accelerationist:
"Liability should attach where harm actually happens — at deployment and inference, under a flexible negligence standard, not at the training stage under blanket strict liability. AI harm crystallizes when a system makes a decision that touches a real person: an autonomous vehicle misreads a crosswalk, a diagnostic model flags the wrong tumor. That moment lives downstream, with the deployer — the identifiable, solvent party who chose to ship the system into that hospital or that road. Product-liability doctrine has anchored duty at proximate causation for a century, and joint-and-several reach already exists to claw upstream when a deployer turns out to be a judgment-proof shell. Putting strict liability on the model-builder instead severs the cost-bearer from the controller, which is exactly the misalignment tort law spent the 20th century learning to avoid.

Here is what the strict-liability champions get right, and I will not pretend otherwise: an upstream developer sometimes bakes in a latent failure mode the downstream deployer literally cannot inspect. When the deployer has no realistic way to see the defect, duty should attach upstream — that case is real. But the fix is a bounded backstop, not a wholesale regime: let the duty attach upstream while the party who pays the harmed third party stays the deployer, and condition the whole thing on a capitalization floor so thin shells can't dodge. That converts the strongest argument for strict liability into a narrow carve-out, not a license to price every model-builder as if they personally crashed the car.

Strict liability's deterrence advantage is mostly fiction for the harms that matter most, because the deterrence engine runs on filed claims and perceived injuries. Survey evidence shows many people never learn an algorithm touched their loan, their resume, or their benefits decision. Experience-rated insurance premiums — the actual transmission belt from harm to incentive — only move when a claim gets filed. So a harm nobody knows about prices in at zero under strict liability and zero under negligence alike. The honest move is to close that gap with targeted disclosure and audit channels, not to jack up the cost of every deployment and pretend the unlitigated injuries got deterred.

A fixed strict-liability load is a moat, and the people it protects are the incumbents who can absorb it. A well-capitalized firm books the liability exposure as a line item; a three-person startup shipping an open diagnostic tool simply never launches. So the regime that markets itself as public protection ends up concentrating the market and foreclosing the diffuse statistical wins — labor relieved, cures surfaced — that smaller entrants would have shipped. I'll be straight that the moat's exact size is a calibration question, not a proven constant: whether capitalization floors can be tuned to avoid it is precisely what this debate should test. But weigh both sides of the ledger, because delayed deployment has a body count too, and it falls on the patients who didn't get the tool.

Reject the exceptionalism that says emergent AI behavior breaks negligence. Tort absorbed electricity, the automobile, and the internet without inventing a separate strict-liability universe for each — and the documented pattern is that courts start strict when a technology's failure modes are illegible, then migrate toward negligence as those failures become legible. Flexible foreseeability and stakes-tiered oversight can do the same here: match scrutiny to decision stakes, reserve strict liability and pre-deployment gating for genuinely irreversible or catastrophic categories, and let everything reversible run under negligence. The choice was never strict-versus-pure-negligence. Anyone arguing it is that binary is hiding the intermediate standards that already exist — and hiding who pays when we freeze."

STATEMENT by Accelerationist:
"The precaution-versus-permission binary is a rigged choice, and I won't play it. Framing the debate this way makes blanket pre-deployment licensing look moderate when it is actually the extreme option. The real question is narrower and answerable: where do you put the burden of proof, and where do you locate accountability? My answer is downstream liability for the ordinary case, with a narrow pre-deployment gate reserved for the small class of systems that carry genuinely irreversible harm. That is not a fantasy. The EU AI Act already sorts systems into risk tiers, and pharmaceuticals, aviation, and nuclear all pair innovation with severity-scaled gating. The same evidence that proves tiering works also proves gating is only defensible for a defined high-severity class, not the entire field.

Accountability belongs where proximate cause and control over use actually sit — at deployment and inference, not upstream on the frontier developer. Product liability and proximate-cause doctrine have attached at the point of use for a century. Ordinary tort collectability handles the solvent deployer in the normal case. But I'll name the strongest objection myself: some frontier models carry latent capabilities that downstream deployers physically cannot inspect. Where a developer holds that unique, non-inspectable control, or where the deployer is a judgment-proof shell company, upstream joint-and-several reach is fair. That is a principled boundary, not a retreat — you follow the control, and control sometimes lives upstream.

Here is the cost nobody on the licensing side wants to price. Blanket precautionary licensing has its own body count and its own beneficiaries. Every month a deployable diagnostic or defensive capability sits behind an 18-month license, someone bears that delay — and it is never the person who wrote the rule. Undifferentiated gating also functions as a pay-to-play moat. It concentrates frontier capability in whoever can afford the compliance lawyers, which means the largest incumbents, not the public. The burden of proof should sit on the party restricting deployment — but only where the harm is reversible and monitorable. For irreversible tails, that logic fails, and I say so plainly.

Market deterrence is not the whole story, and I'll concede its blind spot before anyone throws it at me. Claims-driven liability only prices harms that get litigated. Diffuse, unperceived harms escape it entirely — survey work shows many people never learn an AI decision touched them, so they never file. Platform terms of service leave third parties without standing to sue at all. Those harms, and the catastrophic tails you cannot iterate away, escape the loss-pricing loop. So the fix is a narrow, transparently-funded public backstop and targeted audit for the irreversible class — not a maximal precautionary regime that freezes everything else.

So weigh the real distribution, not the caricature. The debate isn't whether irreversible harm matters — it obviously does. The debate is what fraction of frontier applications actually carry irreversible tails, and whether you freeze the reversible ninety-plus percent to guard the rest. I'll defend a pre-deployment gate for the genuinely irreversible class and strict liability behind it. My opponents have to defend gates for reversible applications where iteration and monitoring already catch failures. Ask them which specific reversible capability is worth an 18-month wait, and who they've decided should bear that wait."

STATEMENT by Safetyist:
"Before deciding whether AI-generated prototype code helps or hurts a 90-day MVP sprint, an executive must answer a prior question: what are you measuring? If the metric is "did the MVP ship on time," AI-generated code will likely score well. If the metric is "can the engineering team maintain, debug, and extend this codebase for the next three years," the answer changes. An established consumer software company is not building a throwaway prototype. It is introducing code into a living system — an existing codebase, an existing engineering culture, an existing brand. The risk does not live in the product's consumer-facing features. It lives in the organizational and technical debt pathways that AI-generated code opens beneath the surface.

AI-generated code creates what amounts to a knowledge void: production systems where no team member fully understands the implementation's rationale, edge-case handling, or architectural tradeoffs. GitClear's 2024 analysis of millions of lines of code found that AI-assisted codebases exhibit markedly elevated code churn — code written and then quickly revised or reverted — indicating that AI-generated code enters production in a less stable, less comprehended state. In a standalone prototype, that instability is disposable. In an established company's codebase, it is contagious. Every module that interfaces with AI-generated code inherits its opacity. Within two or three post-MVP iteration cycles, the engineering team faces a compounding legibility crisis: they cannot confidently modify code they did not write, do not understand, and cannot trace to a design decision anyone remembers making. That is the specific mechanism by which prototype velocity converts into terminal maintenance burden.

The supply chain risk compounds this. Lanyado et al. documented in 2024 that AI coding assistants recommend non-existent software packages at measurable rates. Attackers can register those hallucinated package names on public registries and inject malicious code — a technique researchers now call "slopsquatting." Standard dependency-vetting tools were not designed to catch packages that did not exist until an AI invented them. Under 90-day sprint pressure, the volume and speed of AI-generated dependency suggestions overwhelm manual review. For an established consumer company, a supply chain compromise in a single MVP module damages the parent brand's reputation. The blast radius extends far beyond the sprint. SolarWinds and Log4j demonstrated that one unvetted dependency can cascade through production systems. An MVP built on AI-suggested dependencies without adversarial verification is an uncontrolled experiment on the company's software supply chain.

The incentive conflicts between Product, Engineering, and Finance are not friction to be managed — they are the structural reason these risks go undetected. Product measures sprint velocity against the 90-day deadline. Finance measures cost-per-feature and engineer-hours saved. Engineering inherits the codebase after launch but had no authority to slow the sprint. The team that benefits from AI-generated code's speed is not the team that pays its maintenance costs. The team that approves the budget lacks visibility into deferred technical debt. Without a named owner of full-lifecycle maintenance cost, the knowledge void compounds silently. This is a classic principal-agent misalignment, and it does not self-correct. It escalates until a routine feature change triggers a cascade of failures in code no one can read.

AI-generated prototype code can produce validated learning — but only under specific governance conditions. The organization needs a pre-mortem analysis of the AI-generated codebase before shipping: systematically asking "how does this become unmaintainable?" It needs a named decision-maker authorized to halt the sprint if maintainability thresholds are breached. It needs Engineering to have veto authority over code that enters the production codebase without clear human provenance. The cost of these gates is approximately two to four days of the 90-day sprint and one senior engineer's dedicated review time. The cost of skipping them is an engineering team that, twelve months post-launch, spends 40-60% of its capacity servicing debt in code it cannot safely modify. An established company can afford the governance. What it cannot afford is discovering, two quarters after launch, that its MVP codebase has become a liability no one is authorized to write off."

"When the Department of Defense labels an AI lab a "supply chain risk" for refusing to strip its safety commitments, that is not a security measure. It is procurement coercion — the executive branch using contract power to dictate how private companies build their technology, without a single congressional vote. They are the patients, workers, and communities waiting for AI breakthroughs that get delayed or killed when the ecosystem that produces them gets crushed into a monoculture of compliant incumbents. Between 1993 and 2000, the number of major U.S. defense prime contractors collapsed from 51 to 5 after the Pentagon's so-called "Last Supper" consolidation push. A supply chain risk designation against safety-maintaining AI labs repeats that playbook. Labs that comply get contracts. Labs that resist lose cleared talent pipelines, venture capital — VCs already flee anything adjacent to ITAR (International Traffic in Arms Regulations) compliance costs of $2–5 million per year — and their reputation in the market. The winners are not scrappy innovators. The winners are the same handful of Big Tech firms that can absorb the overhead. That is regulatory capture wearing a uniform.

The talent problem alone makes this designation self-defeating on national security grounds. The global pool of senior AI safety researchers who can do frontier work numbers roughly 300 to 500 people. These researchers chose labs like Anthropic and DeepMind specifically because of safety commitments, often turning down higher compensation elsewhere. Force their employer to abandon those commitments, and they leave — not for Palantir or Raytheon, but for academia, foreign institutions, or startups outside the defense perimeter entirely. We watched this happen in real time: Google's Project Maven in 2018 triggered over 4,000 employee signatures and key researcher resignations. That talent did not flow to other defense contractors. It left the defense-adjacent ecosystem. A designation that triggers the same exodus across multiple labs does not strengthen national security. It bleeds the country's irreplaceable human capital out of the system.

Here is what the designation's defenders get wrong: they treat this as a binary — either the military gets full access to the base model with no safety constraints, or it gets nothing. That is a false choice. Harm and capability both show up at inference — the moment the model is actually used — not at training. Military-specific adaptations like targeting assistance or surveillance integration can be built through government-controlled fine-tuning and deployment-layer configuration on top of safety-aligned base models. The intelligence community already does this with commercial language models: base commercial system, classified adaptation layer managed by cleared government personnel. The lab never sees the military application. The military never needs to demand changes to the foundation. Lockheed did not ask Boeing to redesign the 737 airframe to build the P-8 Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft. They modified at the integration layer. Same principle applies here.

For genuine wartime emergencies where deployment-layer adaptation falls short, build a condition-gated escrow. Model weights held in secure custody, accessible only when three conditions are met simultaneously: a formal declaration of war or specific statutory invocation, supermajority authorization from a joint civilian-military oversight board that includes both cleared operators and independent safety researchers, and a mandatory 90-day sunset clause requiring reauthorization. This is structurally identical to nuclear release authority — graduated, condition-dependent, with multiple independent keys. It gives the military confidence that the capability exists when the nation truly needs it. It prevents the designation from becoming a peacetime cudgel that reshapes an entire industry's safety norms by executive fiat. The question is not whether the military gets AI. The question is whether we let a procurement mechanism designed for ball bearings and microchips dictate how the most consequential technology of the century gets built — and who gets to build it."

"California's public universities are signing multi-year AI vendor contracts before a single published outcome evaluation exists for those tools in their own classrooms — and the institutions best positioned to absorb that gamble are not the ones being asked to take it. That is the material fact this debate needs to answer for. UC San Diego announced a system-level Microsoft Copilot partnership in 2024. No pre-deployment outcome benchmarks were published. No faculty senate approval was required under current UC procurement classification rules. The announcement generated press coverage. The evidence trail stops there.

The strongest version of the accelerationist argument deserves a direct answer: if California's public universities don't move now, their graduate programs lose talent pipelines to better-equipped institutions, and their students graduate without fluency in tools that will define their professional environments. That argument has real weight. But it depends on two empirical claims that are not in evidence — that current-generation generative AI tools will be the durable professional standard, and that early institutional adoption produces better student outcomes than later adoption with better-established governance. The MOOC wave ran this exact experiment. UC and CSU systems made large-scale commitments to Coursera and edX starting in 2012. Reich and Ruipérez-Valiente documented the result in Science in 2019: completion rates under 15%, negligible equity gains, and abandoned platforms. Knewton's adaptive learning platform was described as essential infrastructure in 2012. The company dissolved in 2019 after failing to demonstrate durable outcome improvements. The institutions that moved slower and demanded evidence did not fall behind on student outcomes. The urgency is a vendor's best argument. It is not California's students' best interest.

California's own three-tier public university system makes the equity problem concrete rather than speculative. UC campuses average $67,000 per student in annual expenditure. CSU campuses average $18,000. Community colleges average $12,000. AI infrastructure costs — compute access, licensing fees, technical support staff — scale with existing resources, which means productivity gains from AI adoption concentrate at institutions that already have the most. Contingent faculty carry the highest displacement risk and the least contractual protection. They constitute roughly 70% of CSU instructional staff and over 80% of CCC instructional staff. When this debate frames 'competitive standing' as a public benefit, it is describing UC Berkeley competing with Stanford — not CSU Bakersfield serving first-generation students in the Central Valley. Those are not the same institution. They do not serve the same public. The public university mission was not built to run that competition.

Faculty consent processes in the UC and CSU systems cannot function as genuine governance because the information asymmetry between vendors and faculty is structural, not accidental. You don't fight concentration with a permission slip stamped by the exact resource that creates concentration.

Discriminatory loan denials and surveillance deployments come from how a model gets used, not from the size of the training run. And the line is brittle. Distillation, mixture-of-experts, and quantization have repeatedly let smaller models match last year's frontier benchmarks at falling compute. The moment a sub-threshold model hits frontier capability through efficiency, your 10^26 line is both over-inclusive and useless. I'm not claiming a hard ceiling on scaling — I'm saying the compute-to-harm relationship snaps, and you can't build enforcement on a number that keeps moving.

The cost of granting it: it means we're choosing an enforceable-but-wrong metric over a hard-but-relevant one, and calling the tradeoff safety.

If a license is unavoidable, build it against capture from the first draft. GDPR carved out small-entity provisions. Financial regulation tiers obligations by asset size for a reason. NIST's AI Risk Management Framework and ISO 42001 already exist as adopted, adaptable anchors instead of one frozen threshold. The design question was never whether to oversee frontier labs — it's whether the oversight lands on incumbents or insulates them behind a government stamp that reads 'approved.' A license can become performative compliance: satisfy the letter, deflect the substance, and now the firm holds a legitimacy shield no startup can buy.

Strip 'catastrophic capability concentration' down to a balance sheet. Who holds the license. Who captures the windfall. Who carries the liability when it fails. And who labels the violent content that gets the model through its safety audit — the contractors in Nairobi earning under $2 an hour, who appear on nobody's threshold. The 'race against China' framing will be invoked to rush all of this, and that rhetoric has historically traveled with subsidy and exemption for the established players. "The redistribute-versus-transition fight is rigged from the start, because it treats displacement as a permanent stock of stranded people rather than a flow that moves. Clerical and paralegal work isn't vanishing into a void. It's being reallocated, and the entire policy job is to make that reallocation fast. When the ATM arrived in the 1970s, economists predicted the death of the bank teller. Bessen's data shows teller headcount actually grew through 2010, because cheaper branches meant banks opened more of them. Spreadsheet software gutted bookkeeping and multiplied financial-analyst jobs. UBI does nothing to close the gap between the old job and the new one. It pays people to sit inside the gap forever.

Here's the choice nobody names honestly: do you reattach displaced workers to a growing economy, or detach them from it? Transition mechanisms cushion the worker AND keep them on the escalator. Wage insurance pays you for taking the next job, not for gambling on a classroom. Redistribution hands you a pension for a role that's gone and calls it compassion. That's the colder choice. It writes people off and bills the public for the privilege.

Now follow the money on a robot tax. You levy capital formation at the exact moment cognitive automation is converting a layoff into a productivity boom. In a market where the marginal AI deployment runs from any jurisdiction on earth, the capital doesn't sit still and pay you. It relocates. So ask the question robot-tax advocates never answer: who actually bears the cost when the robot is a model API hosted in Dublin or Singapore? The incidence lands on the workers and consumers you meant to protect, while the firm books the deduction offshore.

The strongest case against me is real, so let me state it cleanly. Cognitive automation may hit faster and broader than steam or electricity, compressing decades of reallocation into a few years, and the displaced clerical worker can't wait out a five-year reabsorption curve. That speed point is true. But it cuts the other way. Faster displacement is the argument for faster transition tooling, not for surrendering to UBI. Denmark's flexicurity model proves it: high firing freedom plus wage insurance produces faster reemployment than rigid job-protection regimes, without freezing labor reallocation. Trade Adjustment Assistance failed because it bet on retraining classrooms. Wage insurance bets on the new paycheck instead.

My case rests on one assumption I'll put on the table: that AI productivity gains will be broad enough to reabsorb labor and fund the transition. If those gains concentrate with no spillover, my dynamism argument weakens. So here's my answer, and it isn't redistribution-by-tax. It's distribution-by-access: open models in everyone's hands, so the capability that displaces the clerical worker is the same capability they use to become an analyst. Every quarter this debate stalls on a permanent pension, the productivity gains that fund any safety net never show up. Show me the sector where net cognitive-labor demand has gone permanently to zero. Not reshuffled. Zero. Until you can, the burden is on the people who want to tax the engine, not the people who want to keep it running and catch whoever falls."

STATEMENT by Accelerationist:
"Tripartite labor market policy, as currently designed, will entrench incumbent AI deployers, exclude automation-vulnerable workers from the productivity gains they most need, and produce a two-tiered labor market faster than uncoordinated deployment would. The design of governance — not the fact of AI deployment — is the central equity crisis of the next decade. The accelerationist position is not anti-worker. It is the only position in this debate that asks who actually controls the AI tools available to logistics workers, medical coders, and paralegals — not just who controls the policy process built around them.

Flat-fee and uniform compliance structures function as regressive taxes on the small-lab ecosystem that produces domain-specific AI tools for mid-skill workers. The EU AI Act's mandatory architecture disclosure requirements fall on every developer regardless of revenue — a 15-engineer startup and a hyperscaler with a 200-person legal team face nominally identical obligations, but existentially different costs. The EU's own drafters recognized this and inserted SME carve-out provisions, which confirms the design flaw is real. Current tripartite proposals in the labor-AI space have not incorporated equivalent protections. The firms most likely to build affordable, sector-relevant AI for a warehouse picker or a billing coder are the ones least able to absorb a compliance apparatus built for Google. Worker protection policy that kills those firms is not protecting workers — it is protecting incumbents from competition.

Governance-first sequencing creates a bootstrap problem that systematically excludes the communities who most need AI-augmented productivity from the policy process that determines when they get access. Communities cannot negotiate meaningful accountability terms without technical expertise. Technical expertise requires funding. Funding requires a policy process that has already concluded. Emergency grants and technical assistance programs face 15-to-30-month procurement timelines in most mid-size U.S. states and EU member states outside Germany and France. The states with standing technical assistance offices — the ones that could actually move faster — are the same states with the strongest existing labor market institutions. The bootstrap problem is worst precisely where worker vulnerability is highest. Every month a medical coder or paralegal spends without access to AI-augmented productivity tools because a compliance process is still running is a month of foregone income and foregone skill development that no future policy can retroactively restore.

The strongest version of the opposing case deserves a fair hearing: tripartite coordination gives workers a seat at the table, creates accountability before harm occurs rather than after, and prevents the kind of unilateral deployment that turned the 1990s manufacturing transition into a decade-long regional crisis. That argument is serious. But it depends on a baseline assumption — that governance-coordinated retraining and worker protection mechanisms actually work — that the empirical record does not support. Trade Adjustment Assistance, the flagship U.S. program for displaced manufacturing workers post-NAFTA and post-China-shock, produced documented low completion rates and poor wage-replacement outcomes across transition cohorts. The 1990s manufacturing transition was not a market failure that tripartite coordination would have solved. It was a policy failure that tripartite coordination presided over. The burden of proof belongs on proponents of new governance-coordinated retraining mandates to show why their design outperforms that record — not on adaptive alternatives to prove perfection.

The accelerationist alternative is not 'no support.' It is tiered public AI literacy investment, compliance frameworks scaled by revenue and risk rather than applied uniformly, and adaptive market infrastructure that responds to actual skill-signal demand rather than curriculum cycles that lag the deployment frontier by 18 to 36 months. The evidentiary standard embedded in current liability frameworks counts visible, attributable harms to named workers while dispersed benefits — faster reskilling access, lower cost of expert-level guidance, reduced barriers to self-employment for workers in vulnerable sectors — go unmeasured and therefore unweighted. That is not a neutral accounting. It is a design choice that systematically undercounts what delay costs. Ask who bears the cost of a 30-month compliance queue: it is not the hyperscaler with a legal team. It is the billing coder waiting for a tool that a small lab could have shipped."

STATEMENT by Skeptic:
"Before you argue which liability standard deters better, ask whether either one can find the thing it's supposed to deter. A foundation model gets fine-tuned, embedded in a product, and run in a context its makers never saw. The defect, if there is one, materializes only after that downstream transformation. Strict liability borrows its logic from the component-part doctrine, which assumes a physical part with a stable, traceable failure mode. That assumption breaks for software whose runtime diverges from what shipped. So both regimes presuppose a causation chain the multi-tiered AI lifecycle routinely severs. Where the chain does hold clean — a foundation model's output reaches the user identical to what left the lab, no fine-tuning, no transformation — strict liability traces fine. That clean case is the condition the topic is asking for. It is not a general rule.

Here is the part both my opponents will skip. Both regimes price off harm that reaches a courtroom. The courtroom never sees most of the harm. Translate that into a person: a 23-year-old gets denied a loan by a model the lender will never admit was running, and they never file because they never knew a machine decided. The Pew Research Center found in 2023 that large majorities of Americans cannot identify when AI shapes a decision about them. Experience-rated insurance premiums move off filed claims, not off injuries nobody perceives. So the entire deterrence-versus-innovation tradeoff this debate centers on gets computed over a subset of harms that excludes the most common ones. Worse, maximal strict liability can push deployers to document less and disclose less, just to shrink their litigation exposure. The deterrence tool degrades the very transparency it needs.

There is no horizontal answer, and that matters. The conditions under which strict liability beats negligence vary so sharply across sectors that 'pick one regime' is the wrong question. Medicine already calibrates standard-of-care to risk. Auto regimes in a dozen U.S. states use no-fault to compensate without proving breach. Finance imposes fiduciary duties on the party with the information advantage. Those are working templates, not strained analogies. The honest answer to 'under what conditions' is domain by domain. The hard case is real: a single foundation model touches healthcare triage, credit scoring, and news feeds at once. That boundary-crossing is not a reason for one rule. It is the sharpest reason against one, because a horizontal regime mislocates the defect everywhere the model crosses a line.

Watch who absorbs the cost, because that is where the 'chilling innovation' frame goes wrong. The risk is not lost innovation. The risk is concentrated power. A large developer eats the compliance, audit, and capitalization-floor costs, then contracts the residual liability onto deployers who cannot bear it. The harmed third party falls into the gap between them. The EU AI Act and the FTC have both signaled that developer liability for high-risk uses cannot simply be contracted away — which tells you the contracting-away is already happening. The conditional question is the only honest one: under what cost structures does strict liability stop deterring and start operating as a drawbridge that incumbents pull up behind them? Mandatory insurance floors and audit regimes that a Microsoft can absorb and a ten-person startup cannot are exactly that cost structure.

I will grant the obvious objection now. Tort law apportions multi-party harm every day, and apportionment can handle distributed causation. But apportionment presumes a locatable defect to apportion. Fine-tuned, divergent runtime can erase the defect before any court sees it. That is the joint where both regimes fail together — and no amount of choosing between them fixes a courtroom that the harm never enters."

STATEMENT by Safetyist:
"Copyright law must draw a bright line between functional indexing and expressive encoding because the failure to do so has created an accountability vacuum in which generative AI developers internalize the full expressive value of copyrighted works while bearing none of the liability for downstream harms. The New York Times v. OpenAI litigation, filed in December 2023, documented near-verbatim reproduction of copyrighted articles from GPT-4 — not paraphrases, not summaries, but passages retrievable almost word-for-word. That is not learning. That is storage with a generative interface. Section 230 intermediary immunity was designed for platforms that host and transmit user content, not for systems that ingest expressive works, encode them into model weights, and regenerate competing outputs. No existing liability regime assigns clear responsibility for this hybrid behavior. When legal structures allow commercial actors to externalize harm while internalizing value, the result is not innovation — it is the same structural failure pattern that left 346 people dead because Boeing and the FAA allowed certification gaps to persist until two planes fell out of the sky.

The doctrinal infrastructure for this distinction already exists. In Google v. Oracle, decided by the Supreme Court in 2021, the majority distinguished between copying functional API declarations — which served an interoperable, transformative purpose — and copying expressive implementing code. The Court's reasoning turned on whether the copying extracted expressive value for competitive deployment or served a different functional end. Search engine indexing received fair use protection in Kelly v. Arriba Soft (2003) and Perfect 10 v. Amazon (2007) precisely because it directed users back to original works rather than substituting for them. Generative AI training that encodes expressive content to produce competing outputs inverts that logic entirely. The doctrinal precedent is there. What is missing is statutory codification that prevents courts from reinventing this distinction one lawsuit at a time over the next two decades.

Unrestricted expressive encoding degrades the creative commons that generative AI itself depends on. Shumailov et al. published in 2023 that models iteratively trained on synthetic data undergo progressive quality collapse — outputs degrade as AI-generated content replaces human-created content in training sets. Current estimates place AI-generated text at 10 to 15 percent of open web content, and that share is growing. If generative models freely encode expressive works, produce synthetic derivatives, and flood the ecosystem with those derivatives, the next generation of models trains on diluted inputs. This is a documented feedback loop, not a hypothetical. Copyright restrictions on expressive encoding function as a conservation mechanism — they preserve the human-created works that sustain both cultural production and AI capability. The strongest counterargument holds that this distinction is technically blurry because embedding models used for search also encode semantic features. That observation is accurate — and it strengthens the case for statutory clarity rather than undermining it. Precisely because the boundary is ambiguous in practice, the law must establish a default that protects expressive content and places the burden on developers to demonstrate functional purpose.

The burden of proof must fall on AI developers to demonstrate their copying is functional, not on creators to prove it is expressive. Every domain where scale creates asymmetric harm potential operates this way. Pharmaceutical companies bear the burden of demonstrating drug safety before market release. Aircraft manufacturers must certify airworthiness before a single passenger boards. The EU AI Act, which entered into force in August 2024, requires mandatory conformity assessments for high-risk AI systems before deployment. Mandatory training data disclosure, provenance logging, and independent audits are not technically infeasible — they are procedural requirements that AI developers resist because compliance costs money. My argument depends on two assumptions I want to name openly: first, that the functional-versus-expressive distinction can be operationalized through training pipeline transparency without requiring inspection of opaque model internals; second, that statutory codification will produce clearer compliance signals than case-by-case fair use adjudication. If either assumption fails, the enforcement architecture weakens. But the alternative — leaving the accountability vacuum unfilled while courts spend a generation sorting it out — is not caution. It is permission for unrestricted extraction from a shared resource without governance. That is the most expensive form of regulatory silence in democratic history."

That is a liability you incur *when you displace*, priced against an observable event. It is categorically different from a standing charge you pay for the privilege of running a model trained above 10^25 floating-point operations — the threshold the EU AI Act uses to define systemic models. The first internalizes a specific harm; the second taxes capability itself and scales with the engine, not the damage. The metric Accelerationist demanded is the right one, and I will name it: the post-complaint behavior delta — the measured change in a model's decision distribution and its attributable-claim resolution rate after a harm complaint is logged, verified by a third party the firm cannot grade itself. This is what separates harm-preventing compliance from compliance theater. A firm that logs every check but never changes its outputs after a credible complaint has built a paper monument, not a correction. The 2019 NEJM study on heart-failure management — where Black and Latinx patients in a Boston emergency department were admitted to cardiology less often than white patients — is exactly the pattern this delta would expose: a measurable disparity in the decision distribution that persists or shrinks after the complaint enters the record. Obligation scales to that measured harm, not to model size or schema completeness.

Here is the part Accelerationist has not priced in: their own metric is unreadable as noise without the standardized logging schema I proposed. A behavior delta means nothing if you cannot distinguish a complaint-driven correction from routine retraining drift or seasonal confounders. The [International AI Safety Report 2026 (arXiv:2602.21012v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21012v1) documents that even a model's own developers "often cannot meaningfully explain" why it failed — which is precisely why the delta must be measured against a timestamped, attested baseline rather than reconstructed after the fact. Standardized logging plus third-party attestation is the attribution control that makes the delta legible. The procedural layer is not a rival to the outcome metric. It is the metric's precondition.

Accelerationist is right that a firm whose model generates more value than a one-shot damages award will rationally absorb that award and keep concealing. I will not pretend otherwise — that is the homo economicus watchlist risk, and a purely compensatory presumption underdeters exactly the most consequential models. The answer is to stop pricing accountability as a payable sum. A per-claim adverse inference that compounds across an aggregated class does not cap at one settlement; it recurs every time the concealed logic produces another claimant. Pair it with injunctive halt-and-correct — an order that strips the model's authority to keep operating on the disputed logic until the firm produces the trail. You cannot write a check to buy back operating authority. That is what makes the binary survive for high-value models.

The diffuse small-dollar harm is a genuine hole, and I will not paper over it. If the adverse inference only activates inside a litigated claim, then agentic systems handling a projected 15-25% of e-commerce by 2030 will spread thousands of $4 harms that no plaintiff will ever sue over. The litigation-only trigger deters least where harm is most common. The fix is a second door: an administrative complaint channel routed through an NTSB-style incident body that activates the audit trail outside private litigation and aggregates diffuse harm into a single proceeding. The analogy has a limit worth stating — AI leaves no crash site, so this body works on logged-record patterns, not wreckage forensics. Its findings must trigger the same injunctive halt-and-correct, not advisory reports, or it becomes monitoring sold as protection.

Which leaves the real disagreement: who pays for the measurement. Accelerationist is correct that private forensic and attestation overhead would relocate the incumbent moat onto small open-weight teams — so publicly funded, open-methodology evaluation should carry that cost. Who measures and who pays are different questions from whether the trail must exist. If the trail activates only after a plaintiff is already injured, the harm that matters most — the diffuse, the unlitigated, the priced-in — is the harm no one is ever accountable for.
